item.title: You Want It Darker
item.description:
Leonard Cohen died in November of 2016, a mere few weeks after the release of his last record, You Want it Darker. The homonymous song of that record greatly surprised me, and revealed to me a Leonard Cohen that I was previously unaware of.

When I like the art produced by an artist, I tend to confine my interest to the art, rather than the artist. I guess I learned this lesson as a teenager, after reading a book about Jim Morrison. (No One Here Gets Out Alive, the life and death of Jim Morrison, the first book I bought in my life, using my own pocket money.) Contrary to my expectations, once I was done reading it I decided that there was really nothing to take home from it. This, then, became a broader theme throughout my life: I have always been very weary of cults of personality and I will almost never state that I am a fan of anyone.

Furthermore, in the exceedingly rare case that I may call myself a fan of someone, I will only do so posthumously, because it is only after someone's death that we can be sure that they will not do anything stupid to disappoint us. This is, for example, why I can say with confidence that I am a fan of Bertrand Russel, while I never said that I am a fan of Elon Musk, no matter how much I liked the guy. (And recent developments vindicate my choice amply, to say the least.) Also, Richard Dawkins has certainly earned his laurels, but technically he is on my waiting list for as long as he is still breathing.

So, the way it went with Leonard Cohen is that I have always liked his music, but I have known very little about the man.

  • I have known him as Canadian, but that is the most basic thing you can know about someone.

  • I have known that he owns a home on the island of Hydra, where he spent a part of his life, but that is something that you cannot fail to know about him if you are Greek.

  • I have known that he is Jewish, but I have not known whether he identified as such by religion or by culture, and I have not sought to clarify this, because I would rather leave his personal life alone.

  • I have known him as a leftist, but there are many examples of leftists who were to some degree religious.

  • I have known him as being anti-establishment, but I had no idea whether he considered god as part of the establishment.

  • I have known that he makes some religious references in his songs, and as far as I could tell, the references were sincere.

So, from all that I knew about him, I had no reason to believe that he had any beef whatsoever with religion, or with god in particular.

When I discovered the song You Want it Darker on YouTube I started playing it in the background, intending to do other things while listening to it, but as soon as I realized what the lyrics were saying I jumped in my seat. I listened to it again. And again. I found the lyrics and read them. To my astonishment, I realized that the song was a fierce condemnation and rejection of the Judeo-Christian god.

The criticism in the song is not directed only towards organized religion, or only towards its followers; it is also largely directed to god himself. It is personal. And it is not just a denial; it is anathema. The song competes with old favorites of mine like Dear God by XTC, Orgasmatron by Motörhead, and God Was Never On Your Side, also by Motörhead. I cannot imagine a more poetic way of telling god to, uhm, basically, fuck off.

Acknowledging the fact that Leonard Cohen's lyrics were often enigmatic, and the fact that we tend to interpret enigmatic lyrics according to our own belief systems, I searched around for more information about the song, trying to find out what others are saying about it. Sure enough, various people appear to interpret the song in whatever way suits their prejudices. I found a religious web site where someone is interpreting the song as an affirmation of Leonard Cohen's faith; so, that person listened to the same song that I listened to, and yet took home from it the exact opposite of what I took home. Great, just great.

Clearly, there must be ways of interpreting the song that are right, and ways that are wrong; but how can we tell?

According to Wikipedia, Alexis Petridis, the head critic for rock and pop music at The Guardian described the song as "a menacing critique of religion". But what do critics know, right? And besides, everyone knows that Wikipedia is unreliable, right?

So, let us look at the lyrics, shall we?

Artist: Leonard Cohen Song: You Want It Darker (2016)

If you are the dealer, I'm out of the game
If you are the healer, it means I'm broken and lame
If thine is the glory, then mine must be the shame
You want it darker
We kill the flame

Magnified, sanctified
Be thy holy name
Vilified, crucified
In the human frame
A million candles burning
For the help that never came
You want it darker

Hineni, hineni
I'm ready, my Lord

There's a lover in the story
But the story's still the same
There's a lullaby for suffering
And a paradox to blame
But it's written in the scriptures
And it's not some idle claim
You want it darker
We kill the flame

They're lining up the prisoners
And the guards are taking aim
I struggle with some demons
They were middle class and tame
I didn't know I had permission
To murder and to maim
You want it darker

Hineni, hineni
I'm ready, my Lord

Magnified, sanctified
Be thy holy name
Vilified, crucified
In the human frame
A million candles burning
For the love that never came
You want it darker
We kill the flame

If you are the dealer, let me out of the game
If you are the healer, I'm broken and lame
If thine is the glory, mine must be the shame
You want it darker

Hineni, hineni
Hineni, hineni
I'm ready, my Lord

For those who read the lyrics above and are still unsure, here is an explanation of it all, verse by verse, courtesy of yours truly.

Of course my interpretation may be subject to my own prejudices, so please, by all means, tell me where you think I am wrong.

  • If you are the dealer, I'm out of the game If you are the healer, it means I'm broken and lame If thine is the glory, then mine must be the shame

    These verses constitute outright denial of god: whatever it is that god stands for, Leonard Cohen wants to have nothing to do with it. Also, an allusion is being made to the biblical significance of repeating something three times as signaling a decree that is fully settled and impossible to ignore.

  • You want it darker We kill the flame

    These verses can be interpreted as a pessimistic assessment of what happens as religion keeps demanding a worsening of the human condition, and its followers abide. The flame may allegorically refer to religion's historical opposition to enlightenment, the inescapable conclusion being that religiosity necessarily implies a dumbing down of the world. In this sense, the flame is the same as the one mentioned by another favorite Jew of mine in his own famous scathing critique of superstitious belief: The Demon-Haunted World (Science as a Candle in the Dark) by Carl Sagan. These verses may even, at the same time, be a reference to the singer's own impending death, by way of the famous poem by Dylan Thomas.

  • Magnified, sanctified Be thy holy name Vilified, crucified In the human frame

    "Magnified and sanctified be His great name" are the opening words of the Kaddish, a prayer central to Jewish liturgy and entirely absent from the Christian literature. The crucifixion, on the other hand, is an exclusively Christian thing, entirely absent from the Jewish literature. Thus, these two verses establish a Judeo-Christian rather than purely Jewish or purely Christian perspective. Obviously, Leonard Cohen has an axe to grind with both. This becomes important a bit further down.

  • A million candles burning For the help that never came

    This points out the folly of all those going through the motions of worshiping a god who is entirely absent. It also constitutes the first reference in this song of the great philosophical / theological Problem of Evil, otherwise known as the Epicurean Paradox: how is it possible to reconcile the existence of evil and suffering in this world with the notion of a supposedly omnipotent, omniscient, and omnibenevolent god? (Spoiler: it is not possible.)

  • Hineni, hineni I'm ready, my Lord

    Hineni is a Hebrew word which means "here I am". It is the response given by various important biblical figures, such as Abraham, when called by god in various chapters of the bible. In Leonard Cohen's own words, (from the official You Want It Darker press conference,) it is "a declaration of readiness, no matter what the outcome."

  • There's a lover in the story But the story's still the same

    The lover is obviously Jesus, since a previous verse established a Judeo-Christian rather than purely Jewish context. To say that the story is still the same is to say that the addition of Jesus does not erase the cruelty of the scriptures, nor the cruelty of the god manifested by those scriptures, and it had no effect on the historical cruelty of his followers.

  • There's a lullaby for suffering And a paradox to blame

    The lullaby for suffering has to be a reference to the perverse fascination of the Christian religion with guilt to the point of self-torture. The paradox has to be the famously nonsensical concept of original sin.

  • But it's written in the scriptures And it's not some idle claim

    This is probably stating that all the impossible, wrongful, and inhuman things written in the scriptures cannot be simply brushed aside, and the religion has to be judged by what its own scriptures say.

  • They're lining up the prisoners And the guards are taking aim I struggle with some demons They were middle class and tame

    This is very obviously a reference to the holocaust, and the demons here are probably the conscience of those who witnessed it and yet kept minding their own business, allowing it to go on. It is the second reference in this song to the Problem of Evil.

  • I didn't know I had permission To murder and to maim

    This has to be a reference to several notable accounts in the bible where god explicitly instructs the Israelites to commit wholesale murder against their neighboring nations.

While researching the song I learned a few details about the circumstances under which it was made, which surprised me all the more. During the last year of Leonard Cohen's life, his deteriorating health severely restricted his mobility; so, the living room of his home was turned into a recording studio to allow him to sing while seated or reclining. This means that the record was created while Leonard Cohen was fully aware that his end was near. There is not a shadow of a doubt that when he says "I am ready, my Lord" he is acknowledging his own impending death.

Now, people on their deathbed do not tend to pick that as the best moment to break ties with god. (Or should I say, to burn their bridges with god.) (Or perhaps, should I say, in his case, to napalm-bomb their bridges with god.) So, the making of this song by Leonard Cohen at the very end of his life is, very interestingly, the antithesis of a death-bed conversion.

Perhaps good old Leonard associated with religion during his life purely out of cultural interest, (like my own father did,) which may have given people some false impressions, so perhaps he wanted to set the record straight before departing.

He surely did.

In no uncertain terms.

I take my hat off to him.

The man: Leonard Cohen (Wikipedia) The record: You Want it Darker (Wikipedia) The song: Yow Want it Darker (Song) (Wikipedia)
